messages.content: I want to develop a continual reinforcement learning agent that adapts to hidden dynamics changes without forgetting policies for recurring regimes. What does that goal require?

The agent needs to keep learning as the environment’s dynamics change, even though the changes are not announced. When a regime recurs, it should be able to perform well there again rather than having lost what it learned previously. The goal has two explicit performance requirements: 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts, and retention of at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return under fixed memory and without regime labels.
Does “hidden dynamics changes” mean the agent can never tell that anything changed?

Not necessarily. It means a change in the dynamics is not directly announced to the agent. Adaptation may depend on what the agent can infer through interaction, but the goal does not prescribe how it makes that inference or how reliably it identifies a particular regime.
And what matters about the regimes recurring?

Recurrence makes past learning relevant again. It is not enough to adapt to a new set of dynamics once if doing so leaves the agent unable to perform well when an earlier regime returns. The goal combines adaptation after a switch with preservation of useful prior-regime policies.
Can you unpack the regret requirement without assuming an evaluation setup that I haven’t given?

It is a comparative target for cumulative regret after switches: the agent should achieve 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts. If the reset-agent comparator has post-switch cumulative regret B on a like-for-like comparison, 20% lower would correspond to no more than 0.8B. The goal does not specify a post-switch measurement window, a regret definition, or the number or pattern of shifts.
Why is “matched-budget” important in that sentence?

It qualifies the comparison. The target is relative to reset agents operating under a matched budget, rather than to reset agents with an unspecified or unequal resource allowance. The statement does not say what components of the budget are matched, so those details should not be filled in as though they were already decided.
Does the requirement say that the agent must outperform reset agents at every single switch?

It says to achieve 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts. It does not explicitly specify whether the threshold must hold at each individual switch or for an aggregate across switches. That distinction would need to be defined before treating either reading as an evaluation rule.
What is the separate point of the 90% requirement?

It expresses the retention side of the goal: keep at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return. Faster adaptation after a switch and good performance when a prior regime recurs are related, but the two stated requirements measure different aspects. The 90% figure is a retention threshold for prior-regime normalized return, not a substitute for the post-switch regret comparison.
So is that necessarily a normalized return of 0.90?

No. The wording is “at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return,” which refers to retaining a fraction of that prior-regime measure. It does not, by itself, establish that the absolute normalized-return score must equal 0.90. The precise comparison also depends on how normalized return is defined, and that definition is not provided here.
Could the agent satisfy the retention target simply by storing an unlimited collection of old policies?

The stated condition rules out treating unlimited memory as an assumption: retention must hold under fixed memory. No memory size or representation is specified, so the goal sets a constraint without choosing a way to meet it.
What does “no regime labels” rule out?

It rules out relying on supplied regime labels as part of the stated condition. The agent is meant to cope with unannounced changes and recurring regimes without being told which regime it is in. That does not prescribe a particular way of representing past experience or detecting a change.
Are “unannounced dynamics shifts” and “no regime labels” saying exactly the same thing?

They are closely related but emphasize different limitations. An unannounced shift means there is no explicit notice that the dynamics have changed; no regime labels means the agent is not supplied an explicit identity for the current regime. Keeping both conditions visible helps avoid quietly assuming either a switch signal or a regime identifier.
I also don’t want “without forgetting” to become an unsupported promise of perfect recall.

That is a useful distinction. The goal describes avoiding loss of useful policies for recurring regimes, while its quantitative retention requirement is at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return under fixed memory and no regime labels. It does not assert perfect recall or unchanged performance in every circumstance.
Would low regret after a switch alone establish that the goal has been met?

No. The stated goal includes both the 20% comparative reduction in post-switch cumulative regret and the at-least-90% retention of prior-regime normalized return. A claim about the regret target alone would leave the retention requirement unaddressed, just as a retention claim alone would leave the regret target unaddressed.
What if I phrase this as adapting quickly whenever dynamics change?

That captures part of it, but it would lose important conditions. The changes are hidden and unannounced, regimes recur, and the agent must avoid forgetting useful prior-regime policies. “Quickly” also does not preserve the specified target of 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents.
Then give me a compact statement that keeps the full target intact.

Develop a continual reinforcement learning agent that adapts to hidden, unannounced dynamics shifts while retaining policies useful when regimes recur. Across recurring shifts, it should achieve 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents and retain at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return under fixed memory and without regime labels.
Does that compact statement claim we have already demonstrated either result?

No. It states a development goal and its requirements, not completed results. The two numerical thresholds are targets to achieve; the statement supplies no experimental outcome showing that either has been met.
Is there any specific algorithm implied by the goal?

No particular algorithm is specified. The goal says what the agent should accomplish and under which constraints, but it does not choose an architecture, a memory mechanism, a change-detection procedure, or a policy-update method. Those should remain open rather than being presented as settled features of the agent.
When discussing success, which details should remain explicit rather than being shortened to “it handles nonstationarity”?

Keep the recurrence and lack of announcement explicit, because the challenge is not merely that dynamics can change. Also retain both numerical requirements and their qualifiers: 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts; and at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return under fixed memory and no regime labels. “Handles nonstationarity” alone does not convey those comparisons or constraints.

For the continual reinforcement learning agent, I’d like to use dynamics-prediction errors to trigger context-based retrieval or training of policy adapters, and merge redundant adapters within fixed memory. How do those pieces fit together?

The proposal uses a mismatch between predicted and observed dynamics as a signal that the agent may need to respond. In response, it could use context to retrieve a policy adapter that may be useful again, or train an adapter if retrieval does not provide an appropriate one. Merging redundant adapters is the proposed way to keep the collection within fixed memory. This is a proposed mechanism for adaptation and retention, not an established performance result.
Does a prediction error prove that the dynamics changed?

No. A prediction error indicates that an observation differed from what the dynamics predictor expected; by itself, it does not prove a change of regime. In this proposal, such errors serve as triggers for considering retrieval or training. The node does not specify how large or persistent an error must be to trigger either response.
Why use prediction errors as the trigger if changes are hidden?

Because a prediction error can be observed through the agent’s interaction even when no change announcement is supplied. It gives the agent a possible cue that its current expectations no longer fit what it encounters. The proposal does not assume that the cue perfectly identifies a switch or names the current regime.
What does “context-based” add to retrieving an adapter?

It says retrieval should depend on the context available to the agent, rather than on a supplied regime label. That matters when regimes can recur: the agent may need to make use of previously learned policy behavior without being told that an earlier regime has returned. The proposal does not define the context representation or how a match is determined.
So the context is not secretly a regime label?

The proposal does not provide regime labels. Context-based retrieval means using information available to the agent to inform retrieval; it does not imply an externally provided regime identity. Whether a learned context reliably distinguishes recurring regimes is a question the proposal itself does not settle.
Why retrieve an adapter instead of always training one?

Retrieval offers a way to reuse policy behavior when the current situation resembles one for which an adapter is already available. Training offers a way to respond when an existing adapter is not suitable. The proposal includes both possibilities; it does not say that one must always precede the other, or specify a decision rule between them.
Does “policy adapter” specify a particular architecture?

No. It identifies something that adapts policy behavior, but the proposal does not prescribe its parameterization, how it attaches to a policy, or how it is trained. Those details should not be treated as established by the phrase alone.
If a familiar regime returns, is the intended response necessarily retrieval rather than training?

Retrieval is the part of the proposal that could exploit an adapter retained from a prior occurrence. But the proposal does not guarantee that a matching adapter remains available or that retrieval will select it. It also does not make a rule that recurrence must always lead to retrieval rather than training.
What is the role of merging redundant adapters?

It addresses the fixed-memory condition. If adapters accumulate as the agent encounters changes, retaining every one without limit would conflict with fixed memory. The proposal therefore calls for merging adapters that are redundant, while aiming to preserve useful behavior for regimes that recur. It does not define redundancy or specify a merge operation.
Is ‘redundant’ the same as ‘created during the same regime’?

Not as stated. The proposal calls for merging redundant adapters, but does not equate redundancy with a known regime identity—and the goal explicitly excludes regime labels. It would be premature to assume that adapters should be merged merely because they seem to come from the same regime, or that different regimes necessarily require separate adapters.
Could merging make the agent forget a useful policy?

That is a relevant concern: merging is meant to respect the memory limit, but the goal also requires retention of at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return. The proposal does not establish that any particular merge preserves that level of return. A merge that harms useful prior-regime behavior would work against the retention objective.
And training a new adapter could also affect what remains available later?

Potentially, because the proposal combines training with a fixed-memory collection of adapters. The stated mechanism does not specify how space for a trained adapter is obtained or which adapters are considered for merging. What matters to the goal is that adaptation to changing dynamics must not come at the expense of the required prior-regime retention.
Would the prediction-error trigger, by itself, meet the post-switch regret target?

No such result follows from the proposal alone. The target remains 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts. Using prediction errors to trigger a response describes a possible route to adaptation; it does not demonstrate the specified comparative reduction.
Could we at least say the adapters solve the no-regime-label condition?

The proposal is framed for operation without supplied regime labels: prediction errors can prompt a response, and context can inform retrieval. But it does not establish that the agent will select the right adapter, train an appropriate one, or achieve the retention target without labels. It proposes how to proceed under that condition, not proof that the condition has been overcome.
How should I describe the sequence without inventing a rigid workflow?

You can say that dynamics-prediction errors trigger consideration of a context-based response: retrieving a policy adapter or training one. As adapters accumulate, redundant ones are to be merged to stay within fixed memory. That conveys the relationships in the proposal without specifying an error threshold, a retrieval rule, a training schedule, or a merging criterion.
Is merging supposed to happen at every detected error?

The proposal does not say so. It links merging redundant adapters to the fixed-memory constraint, but it does not state when merging occurs. An error triggering retrieval or training and the need to keep adapters within fixed memory are connected ideas, not a specified one-error-one-merge schedule.
I want to be careful about what ‘trigger’ promises. Does it require immediately changing the policy whenever a prediction is wrong?

No immediate policy change is specified. ‘Trigger’ identifies dynamics-prediction error as the signal for considering context-based retrieval or training of policy adapters. It does not set a response time or say that every incorrect prediction warrants a different policy.
Can you state the proposal plainly while keeping it distinct from the success criteria?

Use dynamics-prediction errors as cues to retrieve policy adapters based on context or to train adapters, and merge redundant adapters so they remain within fixed memory. That is the proposed approach. Its intended setting is a continual reinforcement learning agent facing hidden, recurring dynamics changes without regime labels; whether it reaches the 20% post-switch regret reduction and retains at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return remains unestablished by the proposal itself.
What context similarity threshold should retrieve an existing adapter after an unannounced switch without confusing regimes that have similar one-step predictions?

There is no numerical threshold specified, and the information so far is not enough to choose one. The central difficulty is that similar one-step predictions do not necessarily mean the same adapter is appropriate. A retrieval threshold would need to distinguish contexts that support reuse from contexts that only look alike on that limited signal.
So a close one-step prediction match is not sufficient evidence for retrieval?

Not by itself. Two contexts could produce similar one-step predictions yet differ in ways that matter for policy behavior. Treating that match as conclusive could retrieve an adapter for the wrong regime. The question is what similarity measure would carry enough relevant information to make retrieval defensible; that measure has not been specified.
Would making the threshold very strict avoid that confusion?

A stricter threshold could reduce some mistaken matches, but it could also reject an existing adapter that would have been useful when a regime recurs. The threshold therefore reflects a tradeoff between inappropriate reuse and missed reuse. Its direction of effect is worth considering, but no strictness level can be justified from the stated information alone.
And a permissive threshold would favor retrieval more often?

Generally, yes, for a given similarity measure: a more permissive acceptance rule would admit more candidate matches. That might help reuse, but it could also increase confusion between regimes with similar one-step predictions. Neither outcome is guaranteed without knowing what the context represents and how similarity relates to useful policy behavior.
Does the threshold apply to dynamics-prediction error or to context similarity?

Your question is about the context similarity threshold for retrieving an existing adapter after an unannounced switch. A dynamics-prediction error plays a different role in the proposal: it can trigger consideration of a response. Even if an error prompts that consideration, a separate question remains about whether the current context is similar enough to warrant retrieving a particular adapter.
Could we use a large prediction error as evidence that none of the existing adapters should be retrieved?

The proposal does not establish that inference. A large mismatch with the current prediction could accompany a return to a regime for which a useful adapter exists. Prediction error may prompt reconsideration; it does not, on its own, determine whether an existing adapter matches the new context.
What does ‘without confusing regimes’ require here if the agent has no regime labels?

It means not treating contexts as interchangeable merely because their one-step predictions are similar, when doing so would lead to an unsuitable adapter choice. The agent need not be given a regime name for that distinction to matter. But without labels, the proposal cannot simply rely on a known regime identity to decide whether retrieval is correct.
Are you saying similarity should be defined in terms of policy usefulness instead of prediction accuracy?

Policy usefulness is the reason the distinction matters, but no particular similarity definition has been chosen. Prediction similarity alone may be insufficient when different contexts call for different policy behavior. A context comparison would need to be informative about whether reusing an adapter is appropriate, rather than merely whether a single prediction looks alike.
If we don't know the similarity measure, does asking for its threshold get ahead of ourselves?

It does limit how precisely the question can be answered. A threshold only has meaning relative to a defined similarity measure and acceptance rule. Without those, a number would be arbitrary: the same numerical value could mean different things for different measures.
Is there at least a universal threshold that would work for any context representation?

No universal value follows from the goal or proposal. How much similarity is enough depends on what the context encodes and whether that similarity separates situations where an existing adapter is useful from situations where it is not. The stated question leaves those matters open.
Suppose two regimes have almost identical one-step predictions. Is it fair to say the threshold must distinguish them anyway?

The desired retrieval behavior should avoid confusing them when their difference matters to adapter choice. But a threshold cannot distinguish them using information that fails to distinguish them. If the context similarity is based only on nearly identical one-step predictions, changing its cutoff may not solve the underlying ambiguity.
That sounds like a limitation of the context, not merely of threshold tuning.

Exactly. The question has two parts: whether the context contains enough relevant information to tell useful reuse from misleading resemblance, and where to set an acceptance threshold on whatever similarity measure is used. A threshold can govern a distinction present in the context; it cannot create one that the context does not capture.
Would it be accurate to say that a threshold alone cannot guarantee no mistaken retrievals?

Yes. Even with a specified similarity measure, a cutoff alone would not guarantee that regimes with similar one-step predictions are never confused. The wording ‘without confusing regimes’ expresses the concern the retrieval rule must address, not a guarantee already supplied by the proposal.
How does the fixed-memory constraint affect this question?

The proposal also calls for merging redundant adapters within fixed memory, so retrieval occurs from whatever distinct adapters remain available. That makes it important not to assume every previously encountered context has a separate stored adapter. Fixed memory does not itself specify a similarity threshold or tell us when two adapters are redundant.
Could a strict retrieval threshold conflict with the goal of remembering recurring regimes?

Potentially. If it repeatedly declines to retrieve a useful retained adapter when a regime returns, the agent may fail to benefit from what it preserved. But an overly permissive threshold could select an unsuitable adapter. The goal requires both adaptation after unannounced switches and retention of prior-regime performance, so neither kind of error can be dismissed in advance.
Should the threshold be selected solely to maximize how often an existing adapter is reused?

That would not capture the stated objective. Retrieval frequency is not itself a success criterion; appropriate reuse matters. The relevant targets remain 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts, and retention of at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return under fixed memory and no regime labels. Those targets do not, however, supply a threshold value.
Does ‘after an unannounced switch’ imply the agent knows exactly when the switch happened?

No. It describes the situation in which retrieval would be useful, not an externally supplied switch notification. The agent is meant to respond to hidden dynamics changes, with dynamics-prediction errors proposed as possible triggers. Neither an exact switch time nor a regime label is supplied by that phrasing.
Could you separate the unresolved question from an answer we would be inventing?

The unresolved question is: given a context similarity measure, how similar must the current context be to a stored adapter’s context before retrieval is preferable to treating the situation as not sufficiently matched, especially when different regimes can look alike through one-step predictions? A specific cutoff, measure, or claim that it prevents confusion would be an invented answer at this point.
So what is the most direct answer if someone presses for a number right now?

No defensible numerical context similarity threshold is specified. In particular, one-step prediction similarity alone may not distinguish regimes that call for different adapters. The threshold remains an open question tied to the context representation and to whether retrieval avoids misleading matches while still recognizing useful recurrence.

I have a hypothesis for the retrieval question: a 0.85 cosine threshold on 32-step residual signatures yields under 5% false retrieval and recalls recurring adapters within 40 steps. How should I state it without presenting it as a result?

State it as a prediction: “We hypothesize that using a 0.85 cosine similarity threshold on 32-step residual signatures will produce under 5% false retrieval and recall recurring adapters within 40 steps.” That preserves the threshold, signature length, and both predicted outcomes while making clear that none has been established.
What part of the earlier threshold question does this address?

It proposes a specific answer to what context similarity cutoff might support retrieval after an unannounced switch: 0.85 cosine similarity, applied to 32-step residual signatures. The predicted under-5% false retrieval speaks to avoiding mistaken matches, while recall within 40 steps speaks to finding an adapter when a regime recurs. It addresses the question as a hypothesis, not as a demonstrated solution.
Is the 0.85 a threshold on prediction error itself?

No. In this hypothesis, 0.85 is a cosine similarity threshold on residual signatures. Dynamics-prediction errors are part of the broader proposed approach, but the stated cutoff applies to similarity between signatures, not directly to the magnitude of a single prediction error.
What does the 32-step part mean here?

It specifies the length of the residual signature: 32 steps. The hypothesis therefore does not rest its retrieval decision on similarity between one-step predictions alone. It does not specify the exact contents of the signature, how residuals are represented, or whether the 32 steps must all occur after a switch.
Can we say the 32-step signature distinguishes regimes with similar one-step predictions?

We can say that addressing that ambiguity is the motivation for the hypothesis. We cannot yet say that the signature actually distinguishes those regimes. The predicted under-5% false retrieval is precisely the kind of outcome that would matter to that concern, but it remains a prediction.
How should I interpret a cosine threshold of 0.85 in plain language?

It proposes accepting a match for retrieval when the relevant cosine similarity reaches the 0.85 cutoff, assuming the usual convention that higher similarity indicates a closer match. The number is a similarity cutoff, not a claim of 85% accuracy or an 85% chance that a retrieval is correct. The hypothesis does not provide a fuller matching rule.
And “under 5% false retrieval” is a strict target, right?

Yes. “Under 5%” means less than 5%, not 5% or less. It is the hypothesized false-retrieval outcome, not a measured rate. The statement does not define precisely which opportunities or retrievals would form the denominator for that rate.
Would it be fair to turn that around and say at least 95% of all switches are handled correctly?

No. An under-5% false-retrieval rate does not by itself imply that at least 95% of all switches are handled correctly. The denominator and the treatment of other possible outcomes are unspecified, and correctly handling a switch is broader than avoiding false retrieval.
What exactly is the within-40-steps claim?

The hypothesis says recurring adapters are recalled within 40 steps. That is a proposed time-to-recall bound for recurrence, not an observed timing result. It does not specify how a step is counted relative to a switch or whether the bound is intended to hold for every recurrence or under some aggregate criterion.
Does that mean an adapter has to be recalled in exactly 40 steps?
No. “Within 40 steps” permits recall sooner; it sets an upper bound of 40 steps in the hypothesized outcome. It does not mean the agent waits until step 40.
A 32-step signature and a 40-step recall bound are different numbers. Is that an inconsistency?

Not on their face. The 32 steps describe the residual signature, while 40 steps describe the hypothesized bound on recalling a recurring adapter. They refer to different things. The hypothesis does not specify enough about signature construction or timing to infer a detailed sequence from those two numbers.
Could someone mistakenly read the 40 steps as a guaranteed detection time for every hidden change?

Yes, and that would overstate the claim. The wording is about recalling recurring adapters within 40 steps, not guaranteed detection of every dynamics change. It also remains a hypothesis rather than a guarantee.
Does it say what happens if the changed dynamics do not match any existing adapter?

No. This hypothesis concerns the similarity threshold, false retrieval, and recall of recurring adapters. The broader proposal allows retrieval or training of policy adapters, but the hypothesis does not specify a training decision or an outcome for a regime with no suitable existing adapter.
Why keep both predicted outcomes instead of just reporting the low false-retrieval figure?

They address different risks. Under 5% false retrieval concerns selecting an unsuitable existing adapter; recall within 40 steps concerns making use of an adapter when a regime recurs. A threshold might be cautious about false matches yet fail to retrieve useful adapters promptly. The hypothesis makes a prediction about both, without establishing either.
Does the hypothesis tell us how the residual signatures are compared beyond saying cosine?

Only to the extent that it names cosine similarity and a 0.85 cutoff on 32-step residual signatures. It does not define the residual representation, the signature’s dimensionality, or how stored and current signatures are prepared for comparison. Those missing details should not be silently supplied as facts.
Could I call 0.85 the optimal threshold?

No. The hypothesis proposes 0.85 and predicts two outcomes at that threshold; it does not compare it with other thresholds or claim optimality. Even if the predicted outcomes held, calling the threshold optimal would require a separate basis that is not stated here.
Could I call the false-retrieval rate an experimental finding if I put “hypothesized” elsewhere in the paragraph?

That would risk a misleading impression. Keep the uncertainty attached to the outcomes themselves: the threshold is hypothesized to yield under 5% false retrieval and recall recurring adapters within 40 steps. There are no reported measurements for either outcome in this node.
Does this establish the original 20% post-switch regret target?

No. The hypothesized false-retrieval rate and recall bound are about the adapter-retrieval mechanism. They do not establish 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents across recurring, unannounced dynamics shifts. That comparative performance target remains distinct from this hypothesis.
Nor does it prove the 90% prior-regime return requirement?

Correct. Recalling a recurring adapter could matter for retaining useful behavior, but this hypothesis does not report prior-regime normalized return. It does not establish retention of at least 90% under fixed memory and no regime labels.
Does the fixed-memory condition change the wording of the hypothesis?

The hypothesis can be discussed in the setting of fixed memory, but its stated prediction does not specify how many adapters are stored, which are merged, or how merging affects the signatures. It is best to retain fixed memory as a condition of the broader agent goal without implying that the 0.85 hypothesis has already solved adapter merging.
How does this respond to the concern that two regimes can have similar one-step predictions?

It moves the proposed comparison to 32-step residual signatures and predicts that a 0.85 cosine cutoff will keep false retrieval under 5% while recalling recurring adapters within 40 steps. That is a concrete hypothesis about avoiding confusion without losing timely reuse. It does not yet show that the longer signatures contain enough information to separate every pair of regimes with similar one-step predictions.
If the same one-step prediction can occur in different regimes, would changing the threshold alone necessarily fix the problem?

No. A cutoff helps only if the signatures being compared capture a useful distinction. The hypothesis pairs a particular cutoff with 32-step residual signatures; it is not a claim that any 0.85 threshold, applied to one-step predictions or any other representation, would avoid false retrieval.
Please give me one careful sentence I can use as the hypothesis.
We hypothesize that a 0.85 cosine similarity threshold on 32-step residual signatures yields under 5% false retrieval and recalls recurring adapters within 40 steps after unannounced dynamics shifts.
Does adding “after unannounced dynamics shifts” accidentally claim that every shift is a recurrence?

It need not, but the sentence can be more precise: “We hypothesize that a 0.85 cosine similarity threshold on 32-step residual signatures yields under 5% false retrieval and, when a regime recurs after an unannounced switch, recalls its adapter within 40 steps.” That ties the recall prediction specifically to recurring adapters without treating every switch as a recurrence.

The next activity is to test 0.85 cosine retrieval of 32-step residual signatures on SwitchWalker-12 across confusable regimes, measuring false retrieval and recall latency. What does that test address?

It evaluates the retrieval hypothesis where confusion is a concern. The test applies the proposed 0.85 cosine cutoff to 32-step residual signatures on SwitchWalker-12 across confusable regimes, then measures whether retrieval selects an unsuitable adapter and how long it takes to recall an adapter for a recurring regime. This describes an activity to carry out, not results already obtained.
Why specify confusable regimes rather than just saying we will test retrieval?

The question motivating the hypothesis is whether the agent can retrieve an existing adapter without confusing regimes that can look similar through one-step predictions. Testing across confusable regimes puts that difficulty in view. The activity does not, however, state exactly how confusability is defined or which regimes are included.
Does naming SwitchWalker-12 tell us how many switches or regimes the test contains?

No. SwitchWalker-12 is the named setting for the activity. Its name alone does not establish the number of switches, the number of regimes, or their arrangement, so none of those details should be inferred from it.
What exactly is fixed in the test as stated?

The stated retrieval rule uses a 0.85 cosine threshold on 32-step residual signatures, and the setting is SwitchWalker-12 with confusable regimes. The activity also names two measurements: false retrieval and recall latency. It does not specify the signature construction, a broader matching procedure, or how the measurements are aggregated.
Is the 0.85 cutoff applied to a single dynamics-prediction error?

No. It is a cosine similarity cutoff for retrieval based on 32-step residual signatures. Dynamics-prediction errors motivate the broader approach, but the activity does not describe 0.85 as an error-magnitude threshold or a rule based on one prediction alone.
Would it be accurate to say that this tests whether 32-step signatures avoid the one-step ambiguity?

Yes, as a question the activity is meant to investigate. Measuring false retrieval across confusable regimes can show whether the proposed retrieval rule is prone to mistaken matches in that setting. It would be premature to say the 32-step signatures do avoid the ambiguity before seeing the measurements.
What does false retrieval refer to in this context?

Conceptually, it is retrieval of an existing adapter when that retrieval is inappropriate for the encountered regime. That is the error the hypothesis predicts will be under 5%. The activity says to measure false retrieval, but does not provide an operational definition of an inappropriate retrieval or the denominator for a false-retrieval rate.
If no adapter is retrieved, is that automatically a false retrieval?

No. A non-retrieval is not itself a retrieval of the wrong adapter. It could still matter for the separate question of whether a recurring adapter is recalled promptly. The activity does not specify a full classification of retrieval and non-retrieval outcomes.
And recall latency is about how quickly an existing adapter comes back into use?

It concerns the delay until a recurring adapter is recalled. The hypothesis predicts recall within 40 steps; the activity measures recall latency to evaluate that prediction. The node does not define the exact starting event or the operational criterion for successful recall, so those should not be presented as already specified.
Does measuring latency mean every regime in the test must be a recurrence?

Not necessarily. The activity says to test across confusable regimes and measure recall latency. The hypothesis’s latency claim applies to recalling recurring adapters, but the activity does not describe the full sequence of regimes or say that every switch is a recurrence.
Can we call this an evaluation of the under-5% and within-40-steps predictions?

Yes. False retrieval corresponds to the hypothesis’s prediction of under 5% false retrieval, and recall latency corresponds to its prediction that recurring adapters are recalled within 40 steps. Calling the activity an evaluation of those predictions does not imply that either threshold has been achieved.
Suppose I wrote, ‘SwitchWalker-12 shows that the 0.85 threshold keeps false retrieval below 5%.’ Would that be supported?

No. The node specifies a test and what to measure; it reports no false-retrieval result. The careful wording is that false retrieval will be measured on SwitchWalker-12 to assess the prediction that it is under 5%, not that SwitchWalker-12 has already shown that outcome.
What about saying that recall is guaranteed within 40 steps because we are measuring it?

That would also turn a prediction into an unsupported result. Measuring recall latency lets the activity assess the proposed within-40-steps bound. It does not guarantee that the observed latencies will satisfy it.
Why measure both outcomes in the same activity?

They capture different ways the proposed retrieval rule could fall short. False retrieval concerns confusing one regime with another; recall latency concerns how promptly an adapter is recovered when a regime recurs. Testing across confusable regimes makes it important to consider both mistaken reuse and timely reuse rather than treating frequent retrieval alone as success.
Does the activity compare 0.85 with other cosine cutoffs?

Not as stated. It calls for testing 0.85 cosine retrieval. It neither specifies alternative thresholds nor claims that 0.85 is optimal. The named activity evaluates the stated setting rather than establishing a threshold comparison.
Does it compare the 32-step signatures against one-step prediction matches?

No such comparison is specified. Similar one-step predictions explain the concern about confusable regimes, but the activity names a test of 32-step residual-signature retrieval. It does not explicitly include a one-step baseline or a measured difference between the two.
If the regimes are confusable, is a false retrieval inevitable?

No. ‘Confusable’ identifies the challenge being tested, not an outcome. The activity is meant to measure false retrieval under that challenge. We cannot infer that the proposed rule succeeds or fails just from the fact that the regimes are confusable.
Would the test tell us whether adapter merging works under fixed memory?

The stated activity does not say to test merging or measure memory use. Merging redundant adapters within fixed memory belongs to the broader proposal, but this activity specifically tests retrieval using the 0.85 cutoff and 32-step residual signatures, with false retrieval and recall latency as its named measurements.
Does it directly test the goal of 20% lower post-switch cumulative regret than matched-budget reset agents?

No. The activity does not specify a reset-agent comparison or a cumulative-regret measurement. It tests retrieval behavior that may matter to adaptation after unannounced shifts, but false retrieval and recall latency are not the goal’s post-switch regret result.
Does it directly establish at least 90% of prior-regime normalized return?

No. Recall of an adapter may be relevant to retaining prior-regime behavior, but this activity does not state that prior-regime normalized return will be measured. Its two stated measurements cannot, by themselves, establish the at-least-90% retention requirement.
